name: requests
requirements: I'm a backend developer who calls requests every day. Show me how requests.get() becomes an HTTP request, and where sessions and adapters fit in.

ranking.query: Understand the application architecture, main entry points, core modules, configuration, dependencies, and how to load, process and return data.

questions.question: A maintainer asks a user to run this module before filing an issue. What job does it do for them?
questions.answer: It gathers the platform, Python implementation and installed dependency versions into one report and prints it as JSON
distractors: It checks installed dependency versions and raises an error if any of them is unsupported
It sends a test HTTP request and reports whether the user's network and TLS setup work
It installs any missing optional dependencies so the user can reproduce the bug

So that the import is delayed until the report is printed, which makes the helper start faster

questions.concept: Type guard that is a no-op at runtime
questions.question: A PreparedRequest whose url is still None is passed to is_prepared() in a normal (non-type-checking) run. What happens?
questions.answer: It returns True; the url/method check only exists for static type checkers
distractors: It returns False because url is None
It raises an AssertionError explaining the request was not prepared
It calls prepare() on the request to fill in the missing url
choices: It raises an AssertionError explaining the request was not prepared
It returns True; the url/method check only exists for static type checkers
It returns False because url is None
It calls prepare() on the request to fill in the missing url
questions.explanation: At runtime TYPE_CHECKING is False, so the function skips the url/method check and returns True; the comment says it is a no-op to avoid an AssertionError (src/requests/_types.py:47-52). The check on line 50 is only seen by type checkers, so it never returns False or raises at runtime.

distractors: Objects whose read() returns str instead of bytes
Objects that are not file-like but have a read attribute set to None
Subclasses of SupportsRead that override read with a different signature

Subclasses of SupportsRead that override read with a different signature
Proxy objects that provide read through __getattr__ and so may not pass the protocol isinstance check

questions.question: HTTPAdapter.build_response starts with `assert _is_prepared(req)` and then reads req.url. What does this assert do in practice?
questions.answer: It tells the type checker req is a _ValidatedRequest so req.url and req.method are str, while never failing at runtime
distractors: It stops a request with no url at runtime before a Response is built
It converts req into a _ValidatedRequest instance so later code can rely on url being set
It is how build_response detects a redirect that needs to be re-prepared
choices: It converts req into a _ValidatedRequest instance so later code can rely on url being set
It tells the type checker req is a _ValidatedRequest so req.url and req.method are str, while never failing at runtime
It is how build_response detects a redirect that needs to be re-prepared
It stops a request with no url at runtime before a Response is built
questions.explanation: is_prepared returns TypeIs[_ValidatedRequest], and _ValidatedRequest redeclares url and method as str (src/requests/_types.py:47, 69-79). At runtime it always returns True (line 52), so the assert in src/requests/adapters.py:375 never fires and nothing is converted.

questions.question: adapters.py imports `_types as _t` only inside `if typing.TYPE_CHECKING`, but imports is_prepared from _types at normal runtime. Why the split?
questions.answer: Aliases like TimeoutType and VerifyType are only defined under TYPE_CHECKING in _types.py, but is_prepared is a real function that build_response calls
distractors: is_prepared is defined under TYPE_CHECKING too, so it has to be imported separately
Importing _t at runtime is allowed, but the guard makes start-up faster
_t is only used in docstrings, so it doesn't need a runtime import
choices: Importing _t at runtime is allowed, but the guard makes start-up faster
_t is only used in docstrings, so it doesn't need a runtime import
is_prepared is defined under TYPE_CHECKING too, so it has to be imported separately
Aliases like TimeoutType and VerifyType are only defined under TYPE_CHECKING in _types.py, but is_prepared is a real function that build_response calls
questions.explanation: In _types.py, TimeoutType, VerifyType and CertType are defined inside `if TYPE_CHECKING:` (src/requests/_types.py:55, 140-144), so they don't exist at runtime. adapters.py only uses them in annotations, which `from __future__ import annotations` never evaluates (src/requests/adapters.py:9, 70-74, 132-134). is_prepared is defined at module level (src/requests/_types.py:47) and is called at runtime (src/requests/adapters.py:77, 375).

questions.concept: Static guarantees without changing runtime behavior
questions.question: A reviewer suggests replacing the is_prepared/_ValidatedRequest pattern with plain runtime checks such as `assert req.url is not None` in the adapter. What does the current design give you that this suggestion would lose?
questions.answer: Type checkers see url/method as str after the guard, and runtime behavior stays the same, with no new AssertionError for requests that worked before
distractors: A clearer runtime error when an unprepared request reaches HTTPAdapter.send
A guarantee that PreparedRequest.url can never be reassigned after preparation
A faster connection lookup, because _ValidatedRequest instances are cached by the pool manager
choices: Type checkers see url/method as str after the guard, and runtime behavior stays the same, with no new AssertionError for requests that worked before
A clearer runtime error when an unprepared request reaches HTTPAdapter.send
A guarantee that PreparedRequest.url can never be reassigned after preparation
A faster connection lookup, because _ValidatedRequest instances are cached by the pool manager
questions.explanation: is_prepared is a no-op at runtime precisely "to avoid AssertionError" (src/requests/_types.py:49-52). The narrowing comes from _ValidatedRequest, a subclass that exists only for type checking and redeclares url/method as str (lines 69-79), and it is used before url is consumed in src/requests/adapters.py:375 and 481-483. The trade-off is that no runtime safety is added: there is no clearer error and no immutability, and nothing is cached.

questions.question: GetKwargs adds data and json on top of BaseRequestKwargs, PostKwargs adds only params, and DataKwargs (put/patch) adds params and json. What explains these different additions?
questions.answer: Each TypedDict adds only the options that the matching Session method doesn't already take as named parameters, so no keyword is declared twice
distractors: They record which options the HTTP standard allows for each method, e.g. GET has no params
They restrict which options adapters can forward, so PostKwargs stops data from reaching the adapter
They are runtime validators that reject keyword arguments not listed for that method
choices: They record which options the HTTP standard allows for each method, e.g. GET has no params
Each TypedDict adds only the options that the matching Session method doesn't already take as named parameters, so no keyword is declared twice
They are runtime validators that reject keyword arguments not listed for that method
They restrict which options adapters can forward, so PostKwargs stops data from reaching the adapter
questions.explanation: Session.get takes (url, params), post takes (url, data, json), and put/patch take (url, data) (Session in src/requests/sessions.py). So each TypedDict (src/requests/_types.py:177-188) supplies the remaining options, and shared options sit in BaseRequestKwargs (lines 157-168). These are typing-only TypedDicts for Unpack (lines 55, 155), so they don't validate at runtime or limit what adapters receive.

questions.question: BaseAdapter's send() and close() only raise NotImplementedError. What role does BaseAdapter play in this module?
questions.answer: It defines the contract every transport adapter must fulfil — take a PreparedRequest and return a Response, and clean up — while concrete classes like HTTPAdapter supply the actual connection logic.
distractors: It is a fallback adapter that Requests uses when HTTPAdapter fails, so raising NotImplementedError signals that the request should be retried.
It manages the urllib3 connection pool shared by all adapters, and send() is left unimplemented because pooling happens in __init__.
It is a deprecated class kept only for backward compatibility, and its methods raise to stop anyone from calling them.
choices: It defines the contract every transport adapter must fulfil — take a PreparedRequest and return a Response, and clean up — while concrete classes like HTTPAdapter supply the actual connection logic.
It is a fallback adapter that Requests uses when HTTPAdapter fails, so raising NotImplementedError signals that the request should be retried.
It is a deprecated class kept only for backward compatibility, and its methods raise to stop anyone from calling them.
It manages the urllib3 connection pool shared by all adapters, and send() is left unimplemented because pooling happens in __init__.
questions.explanation: BaseAdapter documents send() as 'Sends PreparedRequest object. Returns Response object.' and leaves send() and close() unimplemented (src/requests/adapters.py:128-155), so it acts as an interface. HTTPAdapter subclasses it and implements them (src/requests/adapters.py:158, 634). Pool management lives in HTTPAdapter.init_poolmanager, not in BaseAdapter (src/requests/adapters.py:239-267).

questions.question: When an HTTPAdapter is unpickled, __setstate__ restores the saved attributes and then calls init_poolmanager again. Why does it need to do this?
questions.answer: The pool manager isn't saved with the pickled state because it can't be pickled, so a fresh one has to be built from the saved pool settings.
distractors: Unpickling corrupts the existing pool manager's sockets, so the old manager must be closed and replaced.
init_poolmanager resets max_retries to its default, which is required after unpickling.
The pickled state contains the original pool manager, but it must be re-registered with the Session before use.
choices: init_poolmanager resets max_retries to its default, which is required after unpickling.
Unpickling corrupts the existing pool manager's sockets, so the old manager must be closed and replaced.
The pool manager isn't saved with the pickled state because it can't be pickled, so a fresh one has to be built from the saved pool settings.
The pickled state contains the original pool manager, but it must be re-registered with the Session before use.
questions.explanation: __getstate__ saves only the names in __attrs__ (max_retries, config and the pool settings), so poolmanager is left out (src/requests/adapters.py:185-191, 223-224). The comment in __setstate__ says it isn't pickleable, and the method rebuilds it from _pool_connections, _pool_maxsize and _pool_block (src/requests/adapters.py:226-237). Nothing in that code touches sockets, resets retries or registers with a Session.

questions.concept: Converting a urllib3 response into a Requests Response
questions.question: After urllib3 returns a raw response, HTTPAdapter.build_response turns it into a Requests Response. Which statement best describes what happens to the data along the way?
questions.answer: Headers are wrapped in a CaseInsensitiveDict, the encoding is taken from those headers, cookies the server set are pulled into the response's cookie jar, and the raw urllib3 object is kept as response.raw.
distractors: The body is read eagerly and decoded into response.text, and the raw urllib3 object is thrown away to free the connection.
Headers are copied into a plain dict with lower-cased keys, and cookies are left on the raw response for the Session to parse later.
The adapter only copies the status code. Headers, cookies and encoding are filled in later by the Session when the user reads them.
choices: Headers are copied into a plain dict with lower-cased keys, and cookies are left on the raw response for the Session to parse later.
The body is read eagerly and decoded into response.text, and the raw urllib3 object is thrown away to free the connection.
The adapter only copies the status code. Headers, cookies and encoding are filled in later by the Session when the user reads them.

Headers are wrapped in a CaseInsensitiveDict, the encoding is taken from those headers, cookies the server set are pulled into the response's cookie jar, and the raw urllib3 object is kept as response.raw.
questions.explanation: build_response creates a Response (from models.py), wraps the headers in CaseInsensitiveDict (from structures.py), sets the encoding from those headers, keeps resp as response.raw and calls extract_cookies_to_jar (from cookies.py) (src/requests/adapters.py:376-395). The body isn't read here: response.raw keeps the urllib3 object, so the 'reads the body eagerly' and 'plain dict' options contradict the code.

questions.concept: Optional dependency fallback for SOCKS proxies
questions.question: A user sets a socks5:// proxy and gets InvalidSchema("Missing dependencies for SOCKS support.") as soon as the request starts. Where should you look first?
questions.answer: At the module-level import of urllib3.contrib.socks. If that import fails, SOCKSProxyManager is replaced by a stub that raises InvalidSchema, and proxy_manager_for calls that stub for any proxy URL that starts with 'socks'.
distractors: At proxy_headers, because it raises InvalidSchema when the proxy URL contains no username for Proxy-Authorization.
At request_url, because it rejects SOCKS proxies for HTTPS requests and raises InvalidSchema.
At cert_verify, because SOCKS proxies need a CA bundle and a missing bundle is reported as InvalidSchema.
choices: At request_url, because it rejects SOCKS proxies for HTTPS requests and raises InvalidSchema.

At the module-level import of urllib3.contrib.socks. If that import fails, SOCKSProxyManager is replaced by a stub that raises InvalidSchema, and proxy_manager_for calls that stub for any proxy URL that starts with 'socks'.
At cert_verify, because SOCKS proxies need a CA bundle and a missing bundle is reported as InvalidSchema.
At proxy_headers, because it raises InvalidSchema when the proxy URL contains no username for Proxy-Authorization.
questions.explanation: The try/except ImportError at src/requests/adapters.py:62-67 defines a stand-in SOCKSProxyManager that raises InvalidSchema (an exception from exceptions.py). proxy_manager_for sends proxies starting with 'socks' to it (src/requests/adapters.py:283-293). proxy_headers only builds an auth header, request_url only picks a URL form, and cert_verify raises OSError, not InvalidSchema (src/requests/adapters.py:331-335).

questions.concept: Extending the transport layer through adapters
questions.question: Your team wants Requests to talk to a new kind of backend (for example, an in-process test transport) without changing the Session's public API. Based on how adapters are designed, what is the cleanest extension point?
questions.answer: Write a class that implements BaseAdapter's send() and close() contract and returns a Response, then mount it on the Session for the URL prefix it should handle.
distractors: Subclass Session and override request() so it skips adapters entirely for the new backend, since adapters are tied to urllib3.
Change HTTPAdapter.init_poolmanager to return a custom manager, because every request must go through HTTPAdapter's urllib3 pool.
Add the new backend as a case inside _urllib3_request_context, since that function chooses which transport handles a URL.
choices: Write a class that implements BaseAdapter's send() and close() contract and returns a Response, then mount it on the Session for the URL prefix it should handle.
Add the new backend as a case inside _urllib3_request_context, since that function chooses which transport handles a URL.
Subclass Session and override request() so it skips adapters entirely for the new backend, since adapters are tied to urllib3.
Change HTTPAdapter.init_poolmanager to return a custom manager, because every request must go through HTTPAdapter's urllib3 pool.
questions.explanation: BaseAdapter defines a transport-agnostic send()/close() contract (src/requests/adapters.py:122-155). HTTPAdapter's docstring shows adapters being attached to a Session with s.mount('http://', a) (src/requests/adapters.py:177-182), and Session exposes mount() and get_adapter() and holds an adapters field. _urllib3_request_context only builds pool-key parameters for urllib3 and doesn't choose a transport (src/requests/adapters.py:85-119), so changing it or forcing the change through HTTPAdapter's pool ties the new backend to urllib3 for no reason.

questions.question: HTTPAdapter.send calls conn.urlopen(..., redirect=False). What would most likely go wrong if someone changed this so urllib3 followed redirects itself?
questions.answer: Redirects would happen inside the transport, out of sight of the session layer, so its own redirect logic (resolve_redirects, rebuild_auth, should_strip_auth, rebuild_proxies) would be skipped and things like credential stripping and per-hop cookies could be bypassed.
distractors: Nothing important, because urllib3 and the Session apply the same redirect rules; the flag only affects performance.
Retries would stop working, because max_retries is ignored by urllib3 whenever redirect handling is enabled.
build_response would crash, because it can only handle responses whose status code is a redirect.
choices: Retries would stop working, because max_retries is ignored by urllib3 whenever redirect handling is enabled.
Nothing important, because urllib3 and the Session apply the same redirect rules; the flag only affects performance.

Redirects would happen inside the transport, out of sight of the session layer, so its own redirect logic (resolve_redirects, rebuild_auth, should_strip_auth, rebuild_proxies) would be skipped and things like credential stripping and per-hop cookies could be bypassed.
build_response would crash, because it can only handle responses whose status code is a redirect.
questions.explanation: The adapter sends exactly one hop and turns it into a Response with the request and cookies attached (src/requests/adapters.py:696-708, 365-401). Redirect policy belongs to the session layer, which has resolve_redirects, rebuild_auth, should_strip_auth and rebuild_proxies on SessionRedirectMixin. If urllib3 followed redirects internally, those hooks would never see the intermediate hops. The retries and build_response options aren't supported by the code: build_response handles any status, with a fallback to None (src/requests/adapters.py:379).

questions.question: A developer creates an HTTPAdapter without passing max_retries and mounts it on a session. The first TCP connection attempt to the server fails. What happens?
questions.answer: The failure is not retried; the adapter is configured with a Retry that allows zero retries, so the error surfaces right away.
distractors: The adapter retries a few times with backoff before giving up, because connection failures are always safe to retry.
The adapter retries indefinitely until the timeout expires, since no explicit retry limit was given.
The adapter retries only if the request was a GET, because GET is idempotent.
choices: The adapter retries a few times with backoff before giving up, because connection failures are always safe to retry.
The adapter retries only if the request was a GET, because GET is idempotent.
The failure is not retried; the adapter is configured with a Retry that allows zero retries, so the error surfaces right away.
The adapter retries indefinitely until the timeout expires, since no explicit retry limit was given.
questions.explanation: When max_retries equals the default, __init__ sets self.max_retries = Retry(0, read=False) (src/requests/adapters.py:208-209), and the docstring states that by default Requests does not retry failed connections (src/requests/adapters.py:168-174). Options describing automatic or method-based retries assume behavior that only appears if you pass a custom value or Retry object.

questions.question: For an https URL, cert_verify is called with verify set to a string path that does not exist on disk. What does the adapter do?
questions.answer: It raises an OSError saying it could not find a suitable CA bundle, before any request is sent.
distractors: It silently falls back to the default CA bundle and continues with verification enabled.
It turns certificate verification off for this connection, because the custom bundle is unusable.
It passes the path to urllib3 as-is and lets the TLS handshake fail later.
choices: It turns certificate verification off for this connection, because the custom bundle is unusable.
It raises an OSError saying it could not find a suitable CA bundle, before any request is sent.
It silently falls back to the default CA bundle and continues with verification enabled.
It passes the path to urllib3 as-is and lets the TLS handshake fail later.
questions.explanation: If verify is not True, the string becomes cert_loc. If that path does not exist, the method raises OSError (src/requests/adapters.py:325-335). The default bundle is used only when cert_loc is empty (src/requests/adapters.py:328-329), so the path is never silently swapped out. Verification is turned off (CERT_NONE) only when verify is falsy or the URL is not https (src/requests/adapters.py:343-346).

questions.concept: Turning a urllib3 response into a Response
questions.question: A server sends the header as `content-type` (lowercase), but application code reads `response.headers['Content-Type']` and it works. Where in the flow from the low-level urllib3 response to the requests Response does this become possible?
questions.answer: In build_response, the adapter wraps the raw urllib3 headers in a CaseInsensitiveDict before assigning them to the new Response.
distractors: Response normalizes header names to title case when its headers property is first accessed.
The server's headers are lowercased by Session before the adapter sees them.
build_response copies the headers into a plain dict, and the Response class lowercases lookup keys itself.
choices: The server's headers are lowercased by Session before the adapter sees them.
build_response copies the headers into a plain dict, and the Response class lowercases lookup keys itself.
Response normalizes header names to title case when its headers property is first accessed.
In build_response, the adapter wraps the raw urllib3 headers in a CaseInsensitiveDict before assigning them to the new Response.
questions.explanation: build_response creates a fresh Response and sets response.headers = CaseInsensitiveDict(getattr(resp, 'headers', {})) under the comment 'Make headers case-insensitive' (src/requests/adapters.py:376-382). The case-insensitive behavior belongs to that data structure and is applied at the adapter boundary, not by Session or by lazy normalization in Response. The same method also attaches the raw response, the URL, cookies and the originating request (src/requests/adapters.py:386-399).

questions.question: A user reports that a request fails with requests' InvalidURL, raised while the adapter is getting a connection (get_connection_with_tls_context), before anything goes over the network. What should you suspect first?

distractors: The proxy URL had no host, because a malformed proxy is reported as InvalidURL.
The server answered with a redirect to an invalid location, and the adapter converted it into InvalidURL.
The CA bundle path was invalid, and certificate errors are reported as InvalidURL.

questions.question: What does _encode_params produce when given the dict {"tag": ["a", "b"], "page": None}?
questions.answer: A URL-encoded string with one pair per list item, "tag=a&tag=b", with the None-valued key left out
distractors: The string "tag=['a', 'b']&page=None", because each value is converted with str()
The original dict unchanged, because only strings and bytes are encoded
"tag=a,b&page=", joining list items with commas and keeping empty keys

The original dict unchanged, because only strings and bytes are encoded
The string "tag=['a', 'b']&page=None", because each value is converted with str()
A URL-encoded string with one pair per list item, "tag=a&tag=b", with the None-valued key left out
questions.explanation: For iterable key/value data, each value that is a list is expanded into separate pairs and values that are None are skipped before urlencode is called (src/requests/models.py:165-178). Only str/bytes and file-like objects are returned unchanged (src/requests/models.py:161-164), so a dict is never passed through as-is.

questions.question: What happens when you call prepare() on a user-created Request object?
questions.answer: A new PreparedRequest is created and filled from the Request's fields; the Request itself keeps its raw inputs and can be prepared again
distractors: The Request converts itself in place into the wire-ready form, so its original fields are replaced
The Request sends itself to the server and returns a Response
The Request copies its fields into a shared PreparedRequest cached on the class

questions.question: A request is prepared with url="https://api.example.com/search?q=x" and params={"page": 2}. How does PreparedRequest build the final URL?
questions.answer: It parses the URL, encodes params through the encoding mixin's _encode_params, and appends them to the existing query with "&", giving ...?q=x&page=2
distractors: The params replace the existing query string, giving ...?page=2
The params are ignored because the URL already contains a query string
The params are stored separately in the body as form data instead of the URL

The existing query is kept, not replaced, and params never go to the body.

questions.question: Someone proposes reordering PreparedRequest.prepare so that prepare_auth runs before prepare_body. What is the main problem this would cause?
questions.answer: Auth handlers receive the request before its body and body-related headers exist, so schemes that need the fully prepared request (e.g. signing) would act on incomplete data, and prepare_body would then overwrite body/length state afterwards
distractors: Nothing changes, because prepare_auth only reads the URL and never touches the request object
Basic auth tuples would stop being converted into HTTPBasicAuth handlers
Cookies would be sent twice, because prepare_auth also generates the Cookie header

Converting a 2-tuple into HTTPBasicAuth happens regardless of order (src/requests/models.py:683-685).

questions.question: When the body is a file-like stream, prepare_body records body.tell() in _body_position, and if tell() raises OSError it stores a fresh object() instead of leaving None. Why this design?

distractors: Because object() is cheaper to store than an integer file offset

Because None would make Content-Length be set to 0 for the streamed body

concepts.name: Path of requests.get() through Session to adapter
concepts.definition: requests.get(url, params, **kwargs) in api.py forwards to request('get', ...), which opens a short-lived sessions.Session() in a with-block and delegates to session.request(); the session is closed afterwards. A Session is the object meant to persist settings (cookies, auth, proxies) across requests, sends PreparedRequest objects and gets back Response objects, and sessions.py imports HTTPAdapter, the transport-level component that works on prepared requests.

concepts.name: Merging session and per-request settings
concepts.definition: sessions.merge_setting(request_setting, session_setting) decides the effective value of a setting: if either side is None the other is used; if both are not mappings the per-request value wins; if both are mappings they are merged with request keys overriding session keys, and keys whose merged value is None are removed.

concepts.name: Adapters work on prepared requests
concepts.definition: An HTTPAdapter operates on a PreparedRequest (a Request after .prepare()), not on the raw arguments to requests.get(). For example, HTTPAdapter.request_url(prepared, {}) derives the path portion of the prepared URL, keeping a leading '//' intact, as shown in tests/test_adapters.py.

items.caption: Start in src/requests/api.py. get() (line 74) does no HTTP work itself: it calls request("get", url, params=params, **kwargs) (line 87). request() then opens a fresh sessions.Session() inside a with-block and returns session.request(...) (lines 70-71). The comment on lines 67-69 explains the with-block: closing the session avoids leaving sockets open. So every module-level call creates and closes its own Session.

questions.concept: Module-level get() delegates to a temporary Session
questions.question: You call requests.get(url, params={'q': 'x'}) without creating any session yourself. What does the library do with that call before any network work happens?
questions.answer: Forwards it to request() with method 'get', which creates a new Session in a with-block and delegates to session.request()
distractors: get() builds the HTTP request bytes itself and writes them straight to a socket
get() hands the call to one global Session that every module-level call shares
get() creates an HTTPAdapter directly and bypasses Session entirely
questions.explanation: get() just calls request("get", url, params=params, **kwargs) (src/requests/api.py:87), and request() does `with sessions.Session() as session: return session.request(...)` (src/requests/api.py:70-71). There is no shared global session, and get() never touches sockets or adapters directly.

questions.question: True or false: two consecutive requests.get() calls share the same underlying Session object, so state from the first call is still there for the second.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Each call goes through request(), which constructs a new sessions.Session() in a with-block and closes it when the block ends (src/requests/api.py:70-71). The second call therefore gets a brand-new Session; thinking they are shared confuses module-level calls with an explicitly reused Session.

questions.question: Why does request() wrap the Session in a `with` statement instead of just creating it and calling session.request()?
questions.answer: So the session is guaranteed to be closed, avoiding open sockets that can cause ResourceWarnings or look like memory leaks
distractors: So the request is automatically retried if the first attempt raises an exception
So the session is locked and the call becomes thread-safe
So the Response is cached and reused by the next call with the same URL
questions.explanation: The comment directly above the with-block says it ensures the session is closed to avoid leaving sockets open, which can trigger a ResourceWarning or look like a memory leak (src/requests/api.py:67-71). Nothing in this code retries, locks, or caches.

items.caption: Next, src/requests/sessions.py. Its docstring (lines 5-6) says a Session manages and persists settings across requests: cookies, auth, proxies. It imports HTTPAdapter from .adapters (line 21), and SessionRedirectMixin declares send(request: PreparedRequest) -> Response (line 132). So a Session sends already-prepared requests and receives Response objects.

questions.concept: Session as holder of persistent settings
questions.question: Your backend service calls the same API many times and needs the same cookies, auth and proxy configuration on every call. Based on sessions.py, which component is designed to carry those settings across requests?
questions.answer: A Session object that you create once and reuse
distractors: The HTTPAdapter, which stores per-user cookies and auth
Each PreparedRequest, which remembers settings from the previous request
The module-level requests.get() function, which keeps settings between calls
questions.explanation: The sessions module docstring states it provides a Session object to manage and persist settings across requests (cookies, auth, proxies) (src/requests/sessions.py:5-6). The adapter is imported as a separate transport component (src/requests/sessions.py:21), and nothing here says a PreparedRequest or module function persists state.

questions.question: SessionRedirectMixin declares `send(self, request: PreparedRequest, **kwargs) -> Response`. What does this tell you about what a Session's send step works with?
questions.answer: It takes a request that has already been prepared into its final form and returns a Response object
distractors: It takes the raw url and keyword arguments exactly as passed to requests.get()
It returns raw socket bytes that the caller must parse into a response
It takes a Response and converts it into the next redirect request
questions.explanation: The declared signature accepts a PreparedRequest and returns a Response (src/requests/sessions.py:132), and both types are imported from models (src/requests/sessions.py:39-45). Raw get() arguments are handled earlier, and the result is a Response object rather than bytes.

items.caption: Put api.py and sessions.py together: module-level helpers create a throwaway Session per call (api.py:70-71), while a Session is what persists cookies, auth and proxies across requests (sessions.py:5-6). Whether you reuse a Session changes what carries over between calls.

questions.question: A script logs in with requests.post(login_url, ...) and the server sets a session cookie. The next call, requests.get(profile_url), is rejected as unauthenticated. What should you suspect first?
questions.answer: Each module-level call uses its own new Session that is closed afterwards, so the login cookie is not carried to the next call; reuse one Session
distractors: CaseInsensitiveDict lowercases the cookie name so the server no longer recognizes it
HTTPAdapter strips all cookies from GET requests before sending them
merge_setting deletes the cookie because the GET call did not pass cookies
questions.explanation: request() creates `sessions.Session()` in a with-block for every call (src/requests/api.py:70-71), while persisting cookies across requests is exactly the Session's job (src/requests/sessions.py:5-6). The other options blame components for behaviour not shown in the code.

questions.question: True or false: replacing repeated requests.get() calls in a loop with one Session reused for every call makes no difference to which cookies, auth and proxy settings carry over between iterations.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Module-level calls build and close a fresh Session each time (src/requests/api.py:70-71), whereas one reused Session persists cookies, auth and proxies across its requests (src/requests/sessions.py:5-6). So reusing the Session does change what persists.

items.caption: merge_setting() in src/requests/sessions.py (lines 76-105) combines a per-request value with the session's value. A None on one side means use the other; non-mapping values (like verify) take the request's value; for two mappings the request's keys override the session's, then any key whose value is None is deleted.

questions.concept: Dropping a session header with None
questions.question: The session setting is {'Accept': 'application/json', 'X-Trace': '1'} and the request setting is {'X-Trace': None}. What does merge_setting(request_setting, session_setting) return?
questions.answer: {'Accept': 'application/json'} - X-Trace is removed and Accept is kept
distractors: {'Accept': 'application/json', 'X-Trace': '1'} because the session value wins
{'X-Trace': None} because the request mapping replaces the session mapping entirely
{'Accept': 'application/json', 'X-Trace': ''} because None becomes an empty value
questions.explanation: Both are mappings, so the session items are copied and then updated with the request items, making X-Trace None (src/requests/sessions.py:96-97); keys whose value is None are then deleted (src/requests/sessions.py:101-103). Accept survives because the request did not override it.

questions.question: A Session-level setting is False and the same setting passed on one request is True (both plain booleans, e.g. verify). What does merge_setting return?
questions.answer: True, because for non-mapping values the per-request value is returned
distractors: False, because the session setting always takes priority
An OrderedDict containing both values
None, because the two values conflict
questions.explanation: Neither value is None, and since they are not both Mappings the function returns request_setting directly; the comment names verify as the example (src/requests/sessions.py:90-94). Dict merging only happens when both sides are mappings (src/requests/sessions.py:96).

questions.concept: None falls back to the other side
questions.question: True or false: if a request passes None for a setting while the session has a value for it, merge_setting returns None and the session value is ignored.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: When request_setting is None the function returns session_setting (src/requests/sessions.py:87-88); likewise a None session setting returns the request value (src/requests/sessions.py:84-85). None at the top level means 'not specified', not 'clear it'.

items.caption: tests/test_adapters.py shows the adapter layer in isolation: a Request is built and .prepare()d into a PreparedRequest, then HTTPAdapter().request_url(p, {}) is asked for the URL to use. For http://127.0.0.1:10000//v:h it must return '//v:h' (issue #6643), i.e. the path part with the leading '//' kept.

questions.concept: Adapter input is a prepared request
questions.question: In this test, what has to happen to the Request before HTTPAdapter.request_url can work with it?
questions.answer: It is converted with .prepare() into a PreparedRequest, which is what the adapter receives
distractors: It is passed to the adapter as a plain Request with only method and url set
It must first be sent through a Session, which returns the object the adapter uses
It is turned into a dict of method, url and headers for the adapter
questions.explanation: The test builds `requests.Request(method="GET", url=...).prepare()` and passes that prepared object to `a.request_url(p, {})` (tests/test_adapters.py:6-8). No Session is involved, and the adapter receives the prepared object, not a dict.

questions.question: For the prepared URL http://127.0.0.1:10000//v:h the test expects request_url to return '//v:h'. What behaviour is the test protecting?
questions.answer: The adapter extracts the path part of the URL and keeps the leading '//' instead of collapsing it or reading it as a host
distractors: The adapter returns the full absolute URL including scheme, host and port
The adapter normalizes '//' to a single '/' before the request is sent
The adapter returns the host and port to connect to, here 127.0.0.1:10000
questions.explanation: The assertion is `"//v:h" == a.request_url(p, {})` (tests/test_adapters.py:8), so the result is only the path with its leading double slash intact; the test name refers to handling leading path separators (tests/test_adapters.py:4). A full URL, a collapsed '/v:h', or a host:port would all fail this assertion.

relations.reason: Knowing how session-level and per-request settings are merged (sessions.py merge_setting) explains what a Session contributes to a call made through requests.get().
sessions.py imports HTTPAdapter and the Session's send step works on PreparedRequest objects; understanding that adapters operate on prepared requests locates the adapter in the requests.get() path.
